title: Used to, was going to, should have
seoTitle: Turkmen used to, was going to: -ardy, -jakdy
intro: [B1 unit 1](b1-u01) built two pasts from a verb form plus `-dY`. This unit uses the same recipe three more times, on forms you already know: the general present `-Ar` gives **used to** (*Öň köp kitap okardym*), the future `-jAk` gives **was going to** (*Saňa jaň etjekdim, ýöne…*), and `-mAlY` gives **should have** (*Ir gelmelidiň*). Last, *bilmek* in the same **used to** form gives **could have** and **couldn't have**: *jaň edip bilerdiň*, *edip bilmezdim*. These are the forms for talking about how things have changed, and about plans and chances that didn't work out.

blocks.text: Take the general present `-Ar` ([A2 unit 4](a2-u04)), add `-dY`, then the past endings: *geler* → *gelerdim*, I used to come; *okar* → *okardym*, I used to read. It tells what happened regularly in the past, as a habit, and often what no longer happens: *Öň köp kitap okardym*, I used to read a lot of books.

rows.en: he or she used to come
you used to come (plural or polite)
he or she used to read
you used to read (plural or polite)

blocks.text: All the rules of `-Ar` come with it: just *-r* after a vowel (*okardym*, *ýaşardyk*); a final *e* becomes *ä* before *-r* (*işlärdim*); and the *t*-verbs soften (*giderdim*, *ederdim*, *aýdardym*).

items.en: I used to read a lot of books.

items.tk: Öň biz bu ýerde ýaşardyk, indi Aşgabatda ýaşaýarys.
items.seg: Öň biz bu ýer|de ýaşa|r|dy|k, indi Aşgabat|da ýaşa|ýar|ys.
items.en: We used to live here; now we live in Ashgabat.

items.tk: Çagalygymda biz her tomus oba giderdik.
items.seg: Çagalyg|ym|da biz her tomus oba gid|er|di|k.
items.en: As a child, we went to the village every summer.
My grandfather used to keep sheep.
My mother used to get up early every day.

blocks.text: **Didn't use to.** The negative of `-Ar` is `-mAz` ([A2 unit 4](a2-u04)), and here it is `-mAz` in every person: *gelmezdim*, I didn't use to come; *okamazdym*, I didn't use to read.

rows.en: he or she didn't use to come
you didn't use to come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Did … use to?** As in every compound past, the particle comes before `-dY`: *gelermidiň?*, did you use to come? *Sen öň Maryda ýaşarmydyň?* Did you use to live in Mary?

rows.en: Did he or she use to come?
Did you use to come? (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Then and now.** `-ArdY` often sits beside the present, with *öň* (before, in the past) and *indi* (now): *Öň çaý içerdim, indi kofe içýärin*, I used to drink tea; now I drink coffee. For a habit you still have, use *heniz hem* (still) with the present: *Atam heniz hem ir turýar*, my grandfather still gets up early.

blocks.title: -ArdY or -ýArdY for a habit?
blocks.text: Both can describe a past habit: *Her gün mekdebe pyýada barardym* and *…barýardym* both mean **I used to walk to school every day**. `-ArdY` has the ring of **used to** and **would**, of memories; `-ýArdY` describes what was going on at the time.

blocks.title: One letter: okardym, okaýardym
blocks.text: *okardym*, I used to read; *okaýardym*, I was reading. Watch the *ýa* of `-ýAr`. And the negative is `-mAz` in every person: *okamazdym*, not `okamardym`.

Add `-dY` and the past endings to the future `-jAk` ([A2 unit 3](a2-u03)): *geljek* → *geljekdim*, I was going to come; *jaň etjek* → *jaň etjekdim*, I was going to call. It looks back at a plan or an intention, very often one that didn't happen: *Saňa jaň etjekdim, ýöne wagtym bolmady*, I was going to call you, but I didn't have time.

rows.en: he or she was going to come
you were going to come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **An ending at last.** The future `-jAk` has no personal ending, so its subject must be said: *Men geljek*. `-jAkdY` has one, like every compound past, so the pronoun can go: *Geljekdim*, I was going to come.

**Wasn't going to.** As with the future, *däl* follows `-jAk`, and here *däl* takes `-dY` and the ending: *geljek däldim*, I wasn't going to come. You will also see the negative inside, *gelmejekdim*. **Was … going to?** The particle comes before `-dY`: *geljekmidiň?*, were you going to come?

rows.en: he or she wasn't going to come
you weren't going to come (plural or polite)
Was he or she going to come?
Were you going to come? (plural or polite)

items.tk: Saňa jaň etjekdim, ýöne wagtym bolmady.
items.seg: Saňa jaň et|jek|di|m, ýöne wagt|ym bol|ma|dy.
items.en: I was going to call you, but I didn't have time.

items.tk: Biz düýn Mara gitjekdik, ýöne otly gelmedi.
items.seg: Biz düýn Mar|a git|jek|di|k, ýöne otly gel|me|di.
items.en: We were going to go to Mary yesterday, but the train didn't come.
Actually, I was going to come.
I was just going to call you!

items.tk: Men gitjek däldim, ýöne dostum meni çagyrdy.
items.seg: Men git|jek däl|di|m, ýöne dost|um meni çagyr|dy.
items.en: I wasn't going to go, but my friend invited me.

blocks.title: A plan, and what became of it
blocks.text: `-jAkdY` usually comes with *ýöne* and the reason the plan fell through: *…ýöne ýatdan çykardym*, but I forgot; *…ýöne ýagyş ýagdy*, but it rained. With *edil häzir* (just now) it says you were about to: *Edil häzir saňa jaň etjekdim!*

blocks.title: Not the plain future
blocks.text: *Saňa jaň etjek* is about the future, **will call you**, and needs its subject: *Men saňa jaň etjek*. For a plan in the past, add `-dY` and the ending: *jaň etjekdim*.

Add `-dY` and the past endings to `-mAlY` ([A2 unit 6](a2-u06)): *gelmeli* → *gelmelidim*. It has two uses. Most often it says what someone **should have** done and didn't: *Sen ir gelmelidiň*, you should have come early. It can also say what someone **was supposed to** do, or **had to** do, at a time in the past: *Men düýn işe gitmelidim*, I was supposed to go to work yesterday; I had to go to work yesterday.

rows.en: he or she should have come
you should have come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Shouldn't have.** *däl* after `-mAlY`, with `-dY` and the ending: *gelmeli däldim*, I shouldn't have come. You will also see *gelmemelidim*. **Should I have?** The particle before `-dY`: *gelmelimidim?*

rows.en: he or she shouldn't have come
you shouldn't have come (plural or polite)
Should he or she have come?
Should you have come? (plural or polite)

items.en: You should have told me in advance.
We should have apologized.
You shouldn't have come here.
Should I have called you?
We should have bought tickets in advance.

blocks.text: **-mAlYdY or -mAlY bolmak?** For **had to** you know `-mAlY bolmak` from [A2 unit 6](a2-u06): *Pyýada gitmeli boldum*, I had to walk, and I did. *Pyýada gitmelidim* says there was the need, or the plan, without saying it happened, and very often it didn't: I should have walked; I was supposed to walk.

blocks.title: One word for should have
blocks.text: English needs three words and a past participle: **should have come**. Turkmen needs one: *gelmelidim*. The person goes at the end, as in every compound past.

blocks.title: -mAlY alone is now or later
blocks.text: *Sen ir gelmeli* is **you must come early** (now, or next time). Only `-dY` puts it in the past: *Sen ir gelmelidiň*, you should have come early.

sections.title: Could have, couldn't have: -(Y)p bilerdi, -(Y)p bilmezdi

blocks.text: You know `-(Y)p bilmek` for **can** ([A2 unit 5](a2-u05)). Put *bilmek* in the **used to** form of this unit and it says what **could have** happened but didn't: *Sen maňa jaň edip bilerdiň!*, you could have called me! The negative, `-(Y)p bilmezdi`, says what **couldn't have** happened: *Sizsiz men muny edip bilmezdim*, I couldn't have done this without you.

rows.en: he or she could have come
you could have come (plural or polite)
he or she couldn't have come
you couldn't have come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: The question, as always, puts the particle before `-dY`: *gelip bilermidiň?*, could you have come? Only *bilmek* changes; the first verb keeps its `-(Y)p`, with its usual changes: *edip*, *aýdyp*, *işläp*.

items.en: You could have called me!

items.tk: Biz awtobus bilen hem gidip bilerdik.
items.seg: Biz awtobus bilen hem gid|ip bil|er|di|k.
items.en: We could have gone by bus too.
I couldn't have done this without you.
My grandfather could have become a doctor.
I couldn't have done it alone.

blocks.text: **Could have or was able to?** *Edip bildim* says what you managed to do; *edip bilmedim* what you didn't manage, on that occasion: both are facts. *Edip bilerdim* and *edip bilmezdim* are about what was possible or impossible, often in a situation that didn't happen: **I could have done it**, **I couldn't have done it**.

blocks.title: A reproach
blocks.text: *Sen maňa aýdyp bilerdiň!*, you could have told me!, is close to *Sen maňa aýtmalydyň*, you should have told me. The first says it was possible; the second, that it was the right thing to do.

blocks.title: Coming later
blocks.text: The **used to** form also gives the **would** of unreal conditions, *Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim* (if I had time, I would come). That use comes with the conditionals in [B1 unit 9](b1-u09).

summary: **Used to**: `-Ar` + `-dY` + the past endings: *gelerdim*, *okardym*, *işlärdim*, *giderdim*; negative `-mAz`: *gelmezdim*; question *gelermidiň?*
**Was going to**: `-jAk` + `-dY`: *geljekdim*; negative *geljek däldim* (also *gelmejekdim*); question *geljekmidiň?* It has an ending, so the pronoun can go.
**Should have, was supposed to**: `-mAlY` + `-dY`: *gelmelidim*; negative *gelmeli däldim*; question *gelmelimidim?*
*gitmeli boldum*: I had to go, and went; *gitmelidim*: I should have gone, or was supposed to.
**Could have, couldn't have**: *gelip bilerdim*, *gelip bilmezdim*; question *gelip bilermidiň?*
In all of them the particle comes before `-dY` and the endings are those of the past.
